strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-supported limitation of prior self-improving preference optimization for T2I generation (SILMM's Best-of-N sampling), backed by a clear preliminary experiment (Figure 2) quantifying the prevalence of semantically indistinguishable winning/losing pairs.

The proposed object-centric pipeline (negative prompt generation via swap/replace/drop, pairwise prompt densification, and self-VQA-based pair selection) is a reasonable and largely self-contained solution that avoids external datasets or auxiliary models, which is appealing for scalability.

Empirical results show consistent and often substantial improvements over both the baseline MLLM (Janus-Pro-7B) and the SILMM baseline across three distinct compositional benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, DPGBench, GenEval), with supporting qualitative examples.

The ablation study is reasonably thorough, isolating the contributions of negative prompt generation, prompt densification, and VQA scoring, and additionally demonstrates that VQA scoring is critical for SILMM's Best-of-N setting but less so for OSPO, adding nuance to the claims.
Extensive appendices provide full prompt templates, VQA question generation strategies, and training hyperparameters, which aids reproducibility and transparency of the self-generated pipeline.
weaknesses: All experiments use a single backbone model (Janus-Pro-7B); despite the discussion section's claim of flexible applicability to other unified MLLM architectures, no evidence is provided testing generalization to other models, limiting confidence in the framework's broader applicability.

The entire pipeline (prompt generation, negative prompt generation, densification, image generation, VQA scoring, and eventual optimization) relies on the same MLLM instance judging its own generations, which risks self-consistent bias and error propagation; no human evaluation or external validation is provided to confirm that the automatically constructed preference labels align with actual human preference judgments.

Category-wise gains are noticeably weaker for Non-spatial and Complex Composition prompts, which the authors attribute post hoc to lower inherent contrast, but no concrete mitigation or deeper analysis (e.g., alternative scoring or perturbation strategies for these categories) is offered.

The preference-strength scoring formula (Eq. 2) divides local score gaps by global score gaps normalized by per-triplet maxima; this ratio could become unstable when global gaps are near zero, and the paper does not discuss numerical safeguards or sensitivity to this design choice.

Results are reported as single numbers without variance/error bars or multiple training runs, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported gains, especially for categories with modest improvements.

The related work and comparison scope is narrow — the only directly compared self-improving baseline is SILMM, and no comparison is made to other preference-optimization objectives (e.g., vanilla DPO) or other selection heuristics beyond Best-of-N, limiting the assessment of which pipeline components are uniquely responsible for gains versus generic effects of any structured negative-pair construction.

The training pipeline involves multiple LLM inference calls per sample (prompt generation, three perturbations, densification, image generation for three candidate pairs, and VQA scoring) which is computationally heavier than simple Best-of-N; the paper claims efficiency from single-iteration training but does not quantify or compare the total computational cost against baselines to substantiate the efficiency claim.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete, well-motivated failure mode of prior self-improving preference optimization (SILMM's Best-of-N sampling): a preliminary experiment (Fig. 2) empirically shows that a large fraction of Best-of-N-derived preference pairs are semantically indistinguishable, providing solid justification for the proposed method.

The proposed object-centric perturbation strategy (swap/replace/drop) combined with pairwise prompt densification is a sensible and reasonably novel mechanism to induce controlled, localized contrasts between winning and losing images without requiring image editing tools or external models/datasets.

The method is validated across three diverse and standard compositional T2I benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, DPGBench, GenEval), with consistent and often substantial improvements over both the base MLLM and the SILMM baseline.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each component (negative prompt generation, densification, VQA scoring), and the paper goes further to test VQA scoring's role under the SILMM Best-of-N setting, showing it is far more critical there than in OSPO — a nice piece of evidence supporting the paper's central hypothesis about explicit contrast vs. incidental sampling variance.

Reasonably good reproducibility support: full prompt templates, hyperparameters, and generation pipeline are documented in the appendix, and the method requires only LoRA fine-tuning (efficient, ~26 GPU-hours), making it practically appealing.

Qualitative examples (Figs. 4, 6-14) and the local/global gap density analysis (Fig. 5) provide converging evidence that the generated preference pairs indeed have larger local contrast while preserving global coherence, matching the paper's design intent.
weaknesses: The framework is only demonstrated on a single base unified MLLM (Janus-Pro-7B). Claims in the discussion about flexible applicability across different model architectures and modalities (video/3D) are speculative and not empirically supported within this manuscript.

No human evaluation is conducted; all preference signals, prompt perturbations, and final benchmark scoring (VQA-based) are generated/evaluated by the same or similar MLLMs, raising a self-consistency/self-bias concern that is not directly addressed (e.g., could the model's own blind spots propagate through negative prompt generation, dense prompt generation, and VQA judging, understating certain failure modes?).

The Preference Strength Score (Eq. 2) involves division by δ (delta) terms without a visible stability safeguard (e.g., epsilon term) for near-zero denominators; the paper does not discuss numerical robustness of this scoring mechanism.

The category-wise performance discrepancies (e.g., limited gains in Non-spatial/Relation categories) are explained post-hoc via a plausible but untested hypothesis (lower inherent contrast) rather than through further diagnostic experiments.
No variance/robustness reporting (e.g., multiple training seeds) is provided, so the stability of the reported gains is unverified.

The discussion acknowledges a tradeoff between object-level contrast and global semantic coherence but does not quantify this tradeoff (e.g., via an explicit global fidelity metric or FID-like image quality measure), leaving the claimed balance only qualitatively supported.

Data/compute cost of constructing the OSPO dataset (three candidate pairs, VQA scoring, densification passes) relative to SILMM's Best-of-N sampling is not directly compared, despite efficiency being a stated motivation.

strengths: Strong motivation via a preliminary experiment that concretely demonstrates the target MLLM's difficulty distinguishing object-level positive/negative image and text pairs, directly justifying the proposed method.

The four-stage pipeline (prompt generation, hard preference pair generation, VQA-based filtering + uncertainty-based selection, object-centric preference optimization) is clearly described and each component is individually ablated (loss terms, filtering/selection, prompt densification), giving good insight into what drives the gains.

Extensive empirical validation across three benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, DPGBench, GenEval) and three different backbone architectures/scales (Janus-Pro-7B, Janus-1.3B, UniTok-MLLM-7B), showing the framework is largely model-agnostic.

Thoughtful analysis of confirmation bias risk from using the same model as both generator and reward estimator, including a comparison against an external VQA model (Qwen-VL-2.5-7B) that shows comparable downstream performance.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, prompt templates, and algorithmic pseudocode (Algorithm 1) are provided in the appendix.
The method requires no external data or reward models, which is a meaningful practical advantage over some competing self-improving/RL approaches that rely on additional supervision.
weaknesses: Results are not uniformly best: OSPO underperforms baselines/competitors on some sub-metrics (e.g., DPGBench 'Other' and 'Entity' categories drop relative to the Janus-Pro-7B baseline or SILMM, and GenEval overall is only second-best among MLLMs), somewhat undercutting the abstract's broad claim of surpassing prior methods and diffusion models across the board.

Comparisons to diffusion-based models are limited to relatively dated baselines (SD-XL, DALL-E 3, FLUX.1); no comparison to more recent, stronger diffusion or unified models, which weakens the claim of surpassing 'diffusion-based specialized image generation models.'

The self-rewarding/self-filtering design creates an inherent risk of confirmation bias; while the authors provide a comparison with an external VQA model, the analysis is fairly narrow (VQA score/hit-rate agreement and one downstream training comparison) rather than a deeper investigation across iterations or failure modes.

Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the framework largely recombines established techniques (SimPO-style preference loss, prompt perturbation, decompositional VQA filtering) into a specific pipeline rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithmic ideas.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated metrics (CLIP-T, VQA-based scores, detector-based spatial scores); no human evaluation is provided to corroborate perceptual image quality or fine-grained alignment improvements.

The pipeline involves many stages and hyperparameters (β1, β2, γ1, γ2, λ1, λ2, λ3, filtering threshold τ, densification, multi-iteration training) that appear to be tuned per backbone, raising concerns about sensitivity and the practical effort needed to reproduce results on new models.

No analysis of the computational/data-generation overhead of the multi-step self-improving pipeline (image/text generation, VQA filtering, uncertainty selection) relative to simpler baselines, which is relevant given the added inference-time cost of steps like Test-Time Scaling used to boost benchmark numbers.

strengths: Well-motivated by a clear preliminary experiment quantifying the base MLLM's inability to confidently discriminate object-level positive/negative pairs, which directly justifies the design choices.

The four-stage pipeline (prompt generation, hard preference pair generation via replace/swap/drop, VQA-based filtering with uncertainty-based selection, and conditional preference loss) is coherent and each component is separately ablated, giving good insight into what drives the gains.

Extensive empirical validation: three benchmarks (T2I-CompBench++, DPGBench, GenEval) and three different MLLM backbones (Janus-Pro-7B, UniTok-MLLM-7B, Janus-1.3B), showing the framework generalizes across architectures and scales.

Thorough appendix analyses including iterative training, test-time scaling, effect of data size, and a dedicated confirmation-bias study comparing self-rewarding vs. an external VQA model (Qwen-VL-2.5-7B), which addresses a natural concern about self-improving pipelines.

The loss ablation offers a genuinely useful insight into the precision/recall trade-off (SimPO alone over-generates objects; adding CoPO/SFT terms improves textual grounding), which is a nontrivial empirical finding.
Strong quantitative improvements over prior self-improving baselines (SILMM, DSR) and even some specialized diffusion models on compositional benchmarks, while operating without external data/models.
weaknesses: On GenEval, OSPO is only second-best overall behind DSR, and the paper's explanation (DSR uses extra supervision) is plausible but not empirically isolated — it would strengthen the paper to control for this more rigorously.

Gains on Non-Spatial/Complex categories are modest and attributed to CLIP-T metric insensitivity; this explanation is asserted rather than independently verified (e.g., via human evaluation or an alternative metric).

The method is a combination of several existing components (SimPO-style loss, decompositional VQA filtering, prompt densification, self-generated hard negatives) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty is primarily in the object-centric instantiation and combination.
No report of variance/statistical significance across runs; all results appear to be single-run point estimates.

The self-rewarding/self-filtering process has an inherent circularity risk (same model generates, filters, and is trained on its own outputs); although a confirmation-bias analysis is included, the ~85% hit-rate agreement with an external model still leaves meaningful divergence unexplained, and downstream training differences are only checked on final benchmark scores, not on qualitative failure modes.

Reproducibility is only moderately supported — the data generation pipeline is very costly (19,000 prompts × 9 images each, multiple MLLM calls for perturbation/filtering/selection), and cost/compute figures for the full self-improving loop are not reported, which may hinder replication by groups with fewer resources.

Baseline comparison breadth is uneven: Table 1/2 include the most thorough baseline comparisons (SILMM, DSR, T2I-R1) only for Janus-Pro-7B, while the UniTok-MLLM-7B and Janus-1.3B experiments in Table 3 lack the same breadth of self-improving baselines, limiting the strength of the generalization claim.
No human evaluation is provided; all evaluations rely on automated VQA/detector/CLIP-based benchmarks, which the paper itself notes can have low sensitivity in some categories.
